preamble: Debuccalization of coda /d/ to a glottal stop [ʔ]. In Lhasa (Standard) Tibetan the Classical Tibetan final -d was lost as an oral stop and replaced by a glottal stop, usually with umlaut fronting of the preceding vowel, as in Bod 'Tibet' > [pʰø̀ʔ]; some transcriptions record vowel length instead of the glottal stop, and Old Tibetan finals are often reconstructed as voiceless. In African American English, word-final /d/ is variably replaced by [ʔ] (glad [glæːʔ]), a sound change that spread with the Great Migration. Glottal replacement of voiced /d/ is far rarer than that of voiceless /t/.

examples.note: Final -d is replaced by a glottal stop and the vowel is fronted by umlaut; Wiktionary transcribes the Lhasa form with vowel length, /pʰøː˩˧˨/.

examples.from: Classical Tibetan པད pad 'lotus' (from Sanskrit padma)
examples.note: Final -d surfaces as a glottal stop, also in the compound ཞབས་པད zhabs pad [ɕʌpɛʔ].
Word-final /d/ varies between [d], [ʔ], glottal-reinforced [ʔd] and deletion; the glottal variant was led by young working-class women in 1960s Washington DC.
Recorded by Putnam and O'Hern (1955) in a Washington DC community, as cited by Farrington (2020).

sources: Farrington, C. (2020). The Great Migration and the Spread of a Supraregional Variant: Glottal Stop Replacement of Word Final /d/ in DC African American Language. University of Pennsylvania Working Papers in Linguistics 26(2). https://repository.upenn.edu/pwpl/vol26/iss2/10
Farrington, C. (2018). Incomplete neutralization in African American English: The case of final consonant voicing. Language Variation and Change 30(3). https://doi.org/10.1017/S0954394518000145
